taxonomyNote: NatureServe lists the primary name as Common Five-lined Skink and notes Howes et al. (2006) and Richmond (2006) found substantial phylogeographic structure suggesting possible cryptic species; Animal Diversity Web text uses the older name Eumeces fasciatus.
fieldMarks: Five yellow to cream stripes of equal width from snout to tail on a dark background; scales smooth and shiny; adults 12.7-21.6 cm.
Hatchlings black with bright blue tails; adult females keep stripes and a gray tail; adult males fade to brown or olive, jaws orange-red in breeding season.
Enlarged row of scales under the middle of the tail.
behavior: Active April-October in the north; spends much time under cover (rotting wood, rock crevices, sawdust piles, foundations) and basks on logs and rocky outcrops.
Eats spiders, millipedes, crickets, termites, grasshoppers, caterpillars, beetles, snails and sometimes small vertebrates.
Males defend territories against other males; females guard eggs in logs or under rocks; tail detaches readily.
habitat: Moist but not wet, wooded or partly wooded areas with abundant cover and basking sites, including forest edges, cleared and burned areas and Great Lakes driftwood beaches.
range: Southern Ontario and the eastern and central United States: from lower Michigan and eastern New York south to northern Florida, west to Wisconsin, Missouri and eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, with isolated populations in Iowa and Minnesota.

lookalikes.name: Southeastern five-lined skink
lookalikes.howToTell: Five-lined skink has an enlarged row of scales under the tail and prefers moister habitats.

lookalikes.name: Broadhead skink
lookalikes.howToTell: Five-lined skink has four labial scales around the mouth; broadhead skink has five.
